extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 18th-century satirical/epistolary fiction; readers interested in humor and social satire
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of an 18th-century epistolary comic/satirical novel (humorous letters and scenes) to appreciate characterization, social critique, and comic effect. The chunk is a narrative-letter excerpt describing incidents, tastes, and manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape-painting excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise of Mr T--'s landscapes: 'His trees not only have a richness of foliage and warmth of colouring, which delights the view; but also a certain magnificence in the disposition and spirit in the expression... His management of the chiaro oscuro, or light and shadow, especially gleams of sunshine, is altogether wonderful... he is so happy in his perspective, and marking his distances at sea, by a progressive series of ships, vessels, capes, and promontories...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative features to look for in landscape painting: richness of foliage, warmth of colouring, a majestic disposition and expressive spirit, masterful chiaroscuro (light and shadow, including gleams of sunshine), convincing perspective and the use of progressive elements to mark distance. The narrator treats absence of these qualities as reason for lack of pleasure; possession of them predicts an artist's future reputation ('will make a capital figure').

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and taste in public amusements
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical standard for public entertainments (Ranelagh, Vauxhall): 'Vauxhall is a composition of baubles, overcharged with paltry ornaments, ill conceived, and poorly executed; without any unity of design, or propriety of disposition. It is an unnatural assembly of objects, fantastically illuminated in broken masses; seemingly contrived to dazzle the eyes and divert the imagination of the vulgar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good amusements should demonstrate unity of design, propriety of disposition, tasteful conception and competent execution rather than mere glare and spectacle. Anti-patterns: over-decoration, disjointed assemblages, reliance on dazzle and glitter to mask poor conception, and spectacles meant only to 'dazzle the eyes' of the vulgar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper conduct in electoral canvassing
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative remark on candidates' behaviour: 'These visits are mere matter of form, which a candidate makes to every elector; even to those who, he knows, are engaged in the interest of his competitor, lest he should expose himself to the imputation of pride... I know nothing so abject as the behaviour of a man canvassing for a seat in parliament--This mean prostration (to borough-electors, especially) has, I imagine, contributed in a great measure to raise that spirit of insolence among the vulgar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard: avoid abject prostration and venal submission when canvassing; such obsequious behaviour is degrading and contributes to broader social corruption. The passage frames insincere, grovelling courting of votes as an ethical and social failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decent dress and decorum for attendants/postilions
rubrics_metrics.description: Social-propriety expectation: Mrs Tabitha's rebuke: 'An't you ashamed, fellow, to ride postilion without a shirt to cover your backside from the view of the ladies in the coach?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attendants exposed to genteel company are expected to be decently dressed and avoid indecency (e.g., cracked breeches, visible nakedness). Anti-pattern: appearing in rags or with clothing failures that scandalize or offend refined sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of a good stable-servant / footman
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical and social qualities listed by Humphry Clinker as his accomplishments: 'I can read and write, and do the business of the stable indifferent well--I can dress a horse, and shoe him, and bleed and rowel him; and... I can make hog's puddings and hob-nails, mend kettles and tin sauce-pans... I know something of single-stick, and psalmody... I can play upon the jew's-harp, sing Black-ey'd Susan... I can dance a Welsh jig... wrestle a fall... and... find a hare when your honour wants a bit of game.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'complete' servant in this depiction combines practical stable-skills (shoeing, grooming, basic veterinary care), domestic handiwork (mending, cooking), entertainment skills (music, song, dance), and physical competence (wrestling, hunting). The catalogue functions as an evaluative checklist for hiring a versatile, useful servant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban improvement vs. social sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative urban critique: although 'London and Westminster are much better paved and lighted than they were formerly' and new streets are 'spacious, regular, and airy', the city is also 'an overgrown monster... which, like a dropsical head, will in time leave the body and extremities without nourishment and support.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard for good urban development: improvements should not produce central overgrowth that depletes rural areas and destroys social balance. Anti-patterns include excessive centralization, luxury-driven demand that depopulates villages and undermines agriculture, and growth that leads to moral and social disorder.
